overview: Third Age Health Services Limited is New Zealand's leading provider of managed primary medical services to the aged care sector, operating across approximately 90+ Aged Residential Care (ARC) facilities nationwide and serving residents in care homes, private hospitals, secure dementia units, and retirement villages. The company employs a network of GPs and Nurse Practitioners who deliver planned, coordinated care to enrolled ARC residents and community general practice patients, funded through a mix of government capitation payments (via Primary Health Organisations) and fee-for-service consultations. Operating entirely within New Zealand, TAH holds an estimated 17% share of the ARC medical services market (as at 31 March 2025) and is growing through a disciplined acquisition strategy targeting small, founder-owned ARC medical services providers.

business_model.summary: TAH generates revenue through two segments: Aged Medical Care Services (ARC, ~62% of FY25 revenue, growing rapidly) and Community General Practice (~38%, growing modestly). Revenue is predominantly recurring in nature — capitation payments flow monthly from PHOs based on enrolled patient counts and patient demographics, while consultation revenue is earned per visit. The business model is asset-light (clinicians operate in client-owned facilities under service contracts) with high operating leverage as the patient base scales. TAH acquires small ARC medical service businesses at modest multiples, integrates them into its national operating model (the 'Third Age Health Way of Working', grounded in Kaizen principles), and uses a proprietary digital clinical portal to drive efficiency and quality.
business_model.customer_type: B2B (aged care facility operators as primary clients; NZ Government / PHOs as primary funders; individual ARC residents and GP patients as end-users)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand. National footprint with concentration in Auckland, Lower North Island (Wellington), Northland, Canterbury, and Bay of Plenty as at September 2025. No foreign operations or currency exposure.

main_competitors: General practice owner-operators serving ARC facilities ad hoc
Larger integrated aged care operators (Ryman Healthcare, Bupa NZ, Summerset, Oceania Healthcare, Metlifecare) — indirect competition as some manage in-house medical services
Geneva Healthcare / locum GP agencies (compete for clinician supply)
Small regional GP networks that service ARC facilities in specific geographies
competitive_position.market_position: Largest dedicated national provider of managed primary medical care to ARC facilities in New Zealand. Estimated 17% market share of the ARC population at 31 March 2025, up from ~12% in FY24, with a stated medium-term goal of 20%. No single competitor operates at equivalent national scale in this specific niche.

moat_factors.description: With 90+ ARC facilities as of FY25 and growing to include Canterbury and Bay of Plenty via the ARC Health and Cicada Health acquisitions, TAH has a clinician network, operating infrastructure, and management system no small-scale competitor can easily replicate. Facility contracts typically have multi-year tenure and high switching costs for operators who value consistency of care.

TAH's Digital Clinical Portal (live in 30+ facilities by H1 FY26) streamlines clinical workflows, reducing admin burden and enabling real-time clinical oversight at scale. Paired with the 'Elder Care Standards' independently audited quality framework, this creates defensible differentiation that larger integrated care operators have not replicated for visiting-clinician models.

moat_factors.factor: PHO contract relationships and regulatory complexity
moat_factors.description: Capitation revenue flows via PHO agreements that are recognised as intangible assets on acquisition. Establishing and maintaining PHO relationships and navigating ARC-specific capitation enrolment rules creates a meaningful barrier for new entrants. TAH's appointment as sole preferred medical services partner by the Aged Care Association New Zealand (announced H1 FY26) reinforces its sector standing.

moat_factors.factor: Clinician network and workforce development pipeline
moat_factors.description: TAH's NP Development Programme (first graduate March 2025), GP training pathways, and competitive flexible work arrangements provide a partially self-sustaining talent pipeline in an otherwise severely undersupplied market. This is a structural differentiator against smaller operators who cannot fund structured training programmes.

The 'Third Age Health Way of Working' Kaizen-based system enables standardised, low-cost onboarding of new facilities and acquisitions. This operational playbook is difficult to replicate quickly and supports margin expansion even as the business grows.

weaknesses: Small absolute scale (~NZ$21M annualised revenue, ~NZ$48M market cap as at June 2026) limits negotiating leverage with Health NZ / PHOs and limits access to low-cost capital
Community GP segment (~38% of revenue) is consistently underperforming relative to the ARC segment and is experiencing enrolled patient attrition due to GP departures
Dependent on a thin clinician labour market — any acceleration of GP retirements or emigration constrains growth more than demand
Minority-owned subsidiaries (EastMed 67%, Hub Aged Care 70%, ARC Health 80%, Cicada Health 70%) create governance complexity and NCI dilution of earnings
NZX small-cap illiquidity limits institutional investor participation and may result in chronic undervaluation

growth_drivers: NZ demographic tailwind: Population aged 65+ projected to reach 1.6 million by 2058 (25% of population), up from ~820,000 today. The 85+ cohort, which generates the most ARC demand, will grow substantially faster. This is a multi-decade structural demand driver that is not cyclical.

ARC market share expansion: TAH targets 20% of the ARC medical services market (from ~17% at March 2025). This represents organic growth of ~3 percentage points, requiring moderate additional facility contracts rather than significant capital. Ongoing interest from ARC facilities 'constrained only by clinical workforce availability' (H1 FY26 commentary).

Bolt-on acquisitions at attractive multiples: TAH has demonstrated a repeatable playbook — Hub Aged Care (April 2024, $742k total consideration, immediately ahead of expectations), ARC Health (September 2025, $1.1M, Canterbury), Cicada Health (September 2025, $0.9M, Bay of Plenty). Founder-owners seeking succession are a large and growing pool. The Chairman has explicitly broadened the acquisition lens to include non-healthcare businesses sharing similar commercial characteristics (recurring revenue, demand tailwinds, niche within a larger value chain).

ARC capitation rate increases: The June 2025 agreement between Health NZ and sector representatives delivered the largest PHO capitation uplift in over a decade — a 9.69% total government uplift (6.43% capitation uplift plus 50% of $30M contingent funding). A new capitation formula taking effect 1 July 2026 is expected to better reflect the demographics and complexity of TAH's patient population (older, higher acuity, greater multimorbidity), which could be materially positive for TAH's capitation revenue per enrolled patient.

Digital Clinical Portal rollout: Portal reached 30+ facilities by H1 FY26 (from 13 at March 2025). Phases 2 and 3 are in development. Each additional facility deployment reduces per-patient administrative cost, improves care quality metrics, and strengthens client retention. In time, the portal could become a basis for performance-based contract pricing.

AI and virtual care: AI transcription in GP clinics reducing documentation load; virtual/telehealth solutions for after-hours ARC coverage. These tools reduce clinician administrative burden and could extend the reach of each clinician, effectively multiplying capacity without proportional workforce cost.

Elder Care Standards adoption: TAH's independently-assessed Residential Care Medical Service Provider Standard creates a quality benchmark for the sector. If adopted more broadly (potentially as a regulatory standard), TAH would have first-mover compliance advantage and enhanced client stickiness.

business.description: The majority of TAH's revenue ultimately flows from Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) either directly as capitation payments via PHOs or as fee schedules for consultations. Any significant reduction in ARC-specific or GP capitation rates, tightening of enrolment criteria, or Health NZ fiscal constraint (Health NZ is under significant cost pressure and was placed under Commissioner control in 2024) would directly reduce revenue and margins. TAH has limited negotiating leverage as a price-taker in the government-funded primary care system.

business.risk: Clinical workforce shortage and wage inflation
business.description: 57% of NZ GPs are aged 50+, over one-third plan to retire within 5 years, 33% of practices are closed to new enrolment as at January 2025, and NZ is projected to be short 300 GPs within a decade. TAH's ARC growth is already explicitly constrained by clinical workforce availability (stated in H1 FY26 Chairman's report). Wage inflation for GPs and Nurse Practitioners is structural. Cost of services (primarily clinician remuneration) represents ~48% of revenue in FY25.

business.risk: Community GP segment underperformance and patient attrition
business.description: The community general practice segment (Hawkes Bay Wellness, Belmont, Ponsonby Medical, Devonport Family Medicine, EastMed) has chronic challenges. Enrolled GP patients declined from 20,609 (FY24) to 20,350 (FY25) to 20,032 (H1 FY26), driven by GP departures and unfilled vacancies. EastMed is the most financially marginal CGU, with goodwill impairment sensitivity flagged in FY25 accounts. The Chairman acknowledged some acquisitions were mistakes in the FY25 annual report.

CEO Tony Wai is central to TAH's operational improvement and acquisition execution. Chairman John Fernandes is a hands-on capital allocator who has shaped strategy. Founder Bevan Walsh (significant shareholder) has disclosed trading intentions. The company is small (~112 clinicians, small management team) and loss of key clinical or operational leaders could be disruptive. H1 FY26 saw an employee departure that triggered forfeiture of share options.

TAH has made four acquisitions in 18 months (Hub Aged Care, ARC Health, Cicada Health, plus historical GP acquisitions). While the ARC acquisitions have performed ahead of expectations, rapid growth in subsidiary count adds complexity. Minority ownership structures (70-80%) require alignment with founder co-owners who remain active operators. EastMed (67%-owned) has been loss-making at the NCI level.

TAH issued a patient communications update in January 2026 relating to the MMH cybersecurity breach in late 2025. MMH is a patient portal used across NZ primary care. TAH's patient data may have been compromised. Direct financial impact is uncertain but reputational risk exists.

financial.description: With ~9.95 million shares and a market cap of approximately NZ$48-50 million (as at June 2026), TAH is a micro-cap with thin trading volumes. Investors may face wide bid-ask spreads and difficulty exiting positions at scale. This also limits TAH's ability to use equity as acquisition currency.

As at March 2025, TAH had $1.15M in ANZ bank loans at floating rates of ~8.05-8.54%. Total balance sheet debt (bank loans plus lease liabilities) is ~$3.6M, conservative relative to EBITDA of $4.7M. The H1 FY26 line of credit drawdown for Cicada Health was promptly repaid. Interest rate risk is modest but real in an elevated rate environment.

Goodwill ($3.2M at September 2025) and other intangibles (PHO agreements, patient databases, enrolled service users: $3.9M) comprise $7.1M of $12.6M total assets. EastMed goodwill has headroom of only $0.2M above carrying value. Any deterioration in EastMed's performance could trigger impairment. Amortisation charges reduce reported NPAT and will increase as the acquisition portfolio grows.

regulatory.risk: Health NZ funding reform and capitation reweighting
regulatory.description: The NZ Government announced in July 2025 that the capitation funding formula (unchanged since 2002) will be revised, with a new formula expected from 1 July 2026. The new formula incorporates age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality, and socioeconomic deprivation. For TAH's patient population (predominantly elderly, high acuity, often in rural or provincial settings), this could be a net positive — but formula changes introduce uncertainty, and transition arrangements are subject to negotiation between Health NZ and the PHO sector.

A Ministerial Advisory Group on aged care funding model changes was expected to report by mid-2026, with implementation in 2027. Any restructuring of how medical services within ARC facilities are funded or contracted (e.g. shifting to bundled ARC operator payments rather than direct GP capitation) could fundamentally alter TAH's revenue model. The government's stated intent is to reduce hospital pressure by strengthening community and ARC care, which is broadly supportive of TAH.

Health NZ's structural reforms have been reducing the number of PHOs. If TAH's PHO partners are merged or consolidated, contract renegotiation could affect capitation rates or enrolment terms. No specific adverse developments identified in the review period.

macro.description: Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora has faced significant fiscal pressure, was placed under Commissioner control in 2024, and has implemented cost-cutting measures across the health system. While Budget 2025 delivered $95M per year in additional primary care funding from July 2025 (including the 9.69% capitation uplift), Health NZ's structural deficit means any future capitation freeze or reduction would directly compress TAH's revenue per enrolled patient.

macro.risk: NZ economic slowdown affecting GP co-payments
macro.description: TAH's ARC business is largely insulated from economic cycles as ARC residents are fully funded by government subsidy. The community GP segment earns some fee-for-service co-payments from patients, which could soften in a recession, but this portion is a small share of total revenue.

execution.description: The community GP segment has experienced three consecutive years of enrolled patient decline. The company has appointed Lucy Wu as Acting General Manager and is implementing leadership and process changes, but stated that 'a meaningful amount of work remains'. If enrolled patient numbers continue to decline, GP segment revenue and profitability could deteriorate further, and goodwill impairment of EastMed becomes more likely.

execution.risk: Acquisition pipeline quality and capital allocation
execution.description: The Chairman acknowledged in FY25 that some past decisions (implied to be some GP practice acquisitions) were mistakes that diverted focus. The stated intent to broaden the acquisition lens beyond primary healthcare to other businesses with similar commercial characteristics introduces execution risk if management ventures into unfamiliar sectors.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ aged care demand is structurally growing driven by demographics. People aged 65+ will increase from ~820,000 today to an estimated 1.6 million by 2058. The 85+ cohort (highest ARC utilisation) will grow fastest. Supply of ARC facilities is constrained by land, construction costs, and staffing, keeping occupancy rates high. Demand for medical services within ARC settings will grow proportionally. The primary care sector faces chronic structural underfunding (capitation formula unchanged since 2002) but is receiving the largest uplift in a decade from FY26. GP supply is structurally deficient and will worsen for at least 5-10 years.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Very low. ARC medical services are non-discretionary healthcare funded primarily by government. Community GP services are partially discretionary (fee co-payments) but predominantly government-funded. TAH's revenue has grown through COVID-19 disruptions and NZ's 2023-24 economic slowdown without interruption.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity. Total floating rate bank debt is ~$1.15M at March 2025, implying less than $12k annual earnings impact per 100bps rate movement (per FY25 sensitivity disclosure). Indirect benefit from lower NZ OCR (NZ OCR declining from 5.5% peak in 2023-24 toward 3.25-3.5% range in 2025-26) reduces ANZ borrowing costs and supports acquisition financing.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: None. TAH operates exclusively in New Zealand. Revenue, costs, and capital structure are fully NZD-denominated.
key_input_costs: GP and Nurse Practitioner remuneration (largest cost, ~46-48% of revenue, structurally rising)
Nurse Practitioner and GP locum rates
Technology and IT infrastructure ($720k in FY25, ~3.8% of revenue)
Lease costs for GP clinic premises ($632k cash outflows FY25)

recent_developments.event: TAH released preliminary unaudited FY26 full-year results (year ended 31 March 2026): NPAT rose 24.7% YoY to $3.1M; underlying NPATA up 25.9% to $3.6M. ARC segment delivered robust revenue and profit growth. Community GP revenue grew modestly but enrolled patients declined 4.8% YoY due to doctor departures and vacancies. Management noted ongoing workforce shortages and cost pressures, and described FY27 operating backdrop as 'difficult'. Current market capitalisation approximately NZ$48.7M.

TAH reported Q3 FY26 performance: NPAT of $818k for the quarter, up 16.7% YoY. Board also declared Q3 FY26 interim dividend of 4.00 cents per share (fully imputed), in line with the fixed quarterly dividend policy adopted from FY26.

TAH released H1 FY26 results (six months to 30 September 2025): Revenue $10.65M (+13.2% YoY), NPAT $1.52M (+31.7% YoY), underlying NPATA $1.74M (+28.0% YoY). ARC enrolled patients 7,159 (including 1,684 from ARC Health and Cicada Health acquisitions); organic ARC enrolled patients grew 3.7% YoY. GP enrolled patients 20,032 (-2.4% YoY). Digital Clinical Portal now live in 30+ facilities.

TAH acquired 80% of ARC Health Limited (Canterbury-based ARC medical services, $1.10M total consideration) and 70% of Cicada Health Limited (Bay of Plenty / Tauranga-based ARC medical services, $0.86M total consideration), both effective 1 September 2025. Both were funded from cash and a brief line of credit drawdown (promptly repaid). Both acquisitions were immediately EBITDA-accretive. Deferred contingent consideration of $280k (ARC Health) and $219k (Cicada) payable September 2026 if performance conditions met.

TAH announced it had developed the 'Residential Care Medical Service Provider Standard' (Elder Care Standards), independently assessed by a Ministry of Health-designated auditing agency. TAH was also appointed as the sole preferred medical services partner by the Aged Care Association New Zealand.

TAH issued a patient information update regarding the Manage My Health (MMH) cybersecurity breach that occurred in late 2025. TAH uses MMH as a patient portal. The company communicated with affected patients and assessed the breach. No material financial impact disclosed.

Health New Zealand and sector representatives agreed to the largest capitation funding uplift in over a decade: 9.69% total government uplift for FY26 (6.43% capitation uplift + 50% of $30M contingent funding), effective from approximately July 2025. This directly increases TAH's capitation revenue per enrolled patient.

NZ Minister of Health announced a revised capitation funding formula (incorporating age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality, and socioeconomic deprivation) to take effect from 1 July 2026. The new formula could increase capitation rates for TAH's older, higher-acuity patient population.

TAH released FY25 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2025): Revenue $19.08M (+26%), NPAT $2.48M (+79%), underlying NPATA $2.89M (+69%), underlying EBIT margin 22.4% (vs 17.2% prior year). ARC facilities grew from 67 to 90 (+34%). Final FY25 dividend of 3.98 cps declared. Board adopted fixed quarterly dividend of 4.00 cps per share from FY26.

TAH acquired 70% of Hub Aged Care Limited (Wellington-based ARC medical services) for $742k total consideration. Hub Aged Care performed ahead of acquisition expectations in its first full year, contributing $1.63M revenue and $523k EBITDA to FY25 results.

guidance.as_of: FY26 Preliminary Results (29 May 2026) and H1 FY26 Report (7 November 2025)

items.notes: FY26 preliminary commentary stated ongoing workforce shortages and cost pressures remain significant risks. After 5 consecutive years of strong growth (revenue CAGR ~35%+ from FY20-FY25), management has explicitly guided to much more modest organic growth. ARC segment expected to continue growing; GP segment remains under pressure.

Q2 FY26 dividend (4.00 cps) declared post H1 period end. Prior FY25 total dividend was 14.71 cps (implying annualised ~14.71 cps vs new fixed 16 cps run-rate, an increase).

items.target: 20% of NZ ARC population within 5 years (medium-term target stated in FY24 annual report)
items.notes: Currently 17% at March 2025. Organic growth constrained by clinical workforce availability. Acquisitions (ARC Health, Cicada Health) contribute incrementally. A new capitation formula from July 2026 may increase funding per patient for TAH's higher-acuity population.

items.target: Ongoing bolt-on acquisitions in ARC and potentially other sectors; no specific deal pipeline disclosed
items.notes: Chairman has widened acquisition lens beyond healthcare to businesses with recurring revenue, demand tailwinds, and niche roles in larger value chains — explicitly targeting founder-owned businesses seeking succession. Deferred contingent consideration payments for ARC Health and Cicada Health ($280k and $219k respectively) due September 2026 if performance conditions met.

guidance.management_commentary: FY25 Chairman's report: 'We are cautiously optimistic that FY26 will build on the progress made in FY25, after several years of strong financial performance, we expect organic growth in both revenue and earnings to be much more modest going forward.' FY26 preliminary results commentary: 'Ongoing workforce shortages and cost pressures remain significant operational risks for FY27, with management expecting a difficult operating backdrop ahead.' H1 FY26: 'We are spending more on workforce recruitment, development and digital enablement to support sustainable growth over time... Our focus remains on what's within our control: delighting customers, running an organisation grounded in Kaizen, aligning incentives and being frugal. We're optimising for long-term durability.'

bull_case: Structural demographic tailwind is among the most powerful and certain long-duration growth drivers in the NZ economy. The 65+ population will roughly double over the next 30-35 years, directly expanding the addressable market for ARC medical services without any competitive innovation required. TAH is the only NZX-listed company specifically positioned to capture this trend as a services provider (not a property owner like Ryman or Summerset).

Market position is being consolidated at attractive valuations. TAH's acquisition multiples have been modest (Hub Aged Care total consideration $742k for a business generating $1.63M revenue and $523k EBITDA; ARC Health and Cicada Health together ~$2M for businesses contributing immediately to EBITDA). These founder-succession acquisitions are integrated rapidly using a proven playbook, generating returns on tangible capital well above cost of capital.

The 2025 capitation uplift (largest in a decade at 9.69%) and forthcoming formula reweighting toward multimorbidity and age from July 2026 should meaningfully increase TAH's capitation revenue per enrolled patient without requiring any volume growth. TAH's patient demographics (elderly, high acuity) are precisely the cohort that benefits most from the formula reweighting.

High and improving profitability metrics: FY25 underlying EBIT margin 22.4% (vs 17.2% in FY24), ROCE 42.8%, ROE 60.9%. Demonstrated operating leverage — revenue grew 26% in FY25 while underlying EBIT grew 64%. The business requires minimal capital expenditure (asset-light clinical services model) and converts a high proportion of EBIT to free cash flow. Even at the moderated FY26 growth pace, TAH generated $3.1M NPAT (FY26E), implying a P/E around 15-16x at current market cap — reasonable for a niche healthcare compounder with a genuine long-duration tailwind.

Appointed as sole preferred medical services partner by the Aged Care Association New Zealand — a powerful endorsement that should accelerate organic facility wins and provide a platform for sector-level advocacy on capitation rates and clinical standards. The Elder Care Standards quality framework, if adopted industry-wide or embedded in regulatory requirements, would create additional switching cost and moat.
bear_case: Organic growth is decelerating and management has explicitly guided to 'much more modest' growth going forward. The FY26 preliminary result (NPAT +24.7%, NPATA +25.9%) is impressive in absolute terms but well below the trajectory of FY25 (+79% NPAT, +69% NPATA). The GP segment is structurally challenged with enrolled patient numbers in ongoing decline, and the Chairman has acknowledged past acquisition mistakes. If the GP segment continues to deteriorate, it consumes management attention and could trigger goodwill impairment.

Health NZ fiscal pressure is the single largest systemic risk. Health NZ was placed under Commissioner control in 2024 amid a significant structural deficit. While Budget 2025 provided a large one-time capitation uplift, TAH remains entirely dependent on government funding decisions. Future capitation freezes, changes to ARC enrolment criteria, or structural reform of how medical services in ARC facilities are funded (e.g. bundled payments to facility operators rather than direct GP capitation) could materially alter the revenue model with little notice.

Clinical workforce shortage is intensifying and is not solvable in the short-to-medium term. ARC growth is already explicitly capacity-constrained. The NZ Government has initiatives (new Primary Care Pathway, third medical school at Waikato from 2027) but supply solutions are 5-10 years away. In the interim, wage inflation for GPs and NPs will compress margins, and competition for clinicians with other providers will intensify. TAH's cost of services (clinician remuneration) is already ~48% of revenue.

Small-cap illiquidity and lack of institutional analyst coverage creates persistent valuation risk. With a NZ$48M market cap and thin trading volumes, TAH stock can be volatile on minimal volume, insider selling (Bevan Walsh established a fixed trading plan in February 2026, with multiple SPH notices filed in 2025-26) could materially impact the share price, and the company cannot access equity capital markets efficiently for larger acquisitions.

Minority ownership structures and NCI complexity could become governance and financial headaches. TAH consolidates 100% of revenue from Hub Aged Care, ARC Health, Cicada Health, and EastMed but owns only 67-80% of each. NCI dividends reduce cash available to parent shareholders. If any minority co-owner (who is typically a founder that remains active) disputes strategy, compensation, or exit terms, disputes could be costly and distracting. EastMed (67% owned) has been loss-making at the NCI level.
